[TASK_TYPE=concept]
[BOUNDARY=rust+crypto]
[SEVERITY=major]
Why is an oracle test against a trusted C reference especially valuable for a Falcon arithmetic component translated into Rust?

Because Falcon arithmetic is numerically delicate enough that compilation success and visually plausible outputs are weak evidence. A trusted oracle gives component-level equivalence checking and can reveal indexing, scaling, sign, or normalization mistakes that ordinary unit tests may miss.

[TASK_TYPE=review]
[BOUNDARY=rust+crypto]
[SEVERITY=major]
A pure Rust Falcon component matches the reference oracle on one fixed input. Is that enough to claim faithful translation?

No. It is a strong first milestone, but not final proof. It establishes that one concrete path matches the oracle, but the audit should still ask for multiple inputs, inverse or roundtrip checks when applicable, and review of precision-sensitive edge behavior.

[TASK_TYPE=audit]
[BOUNDARY=rust+crypto]
[SEVERITY=critical]
A Rust Falcon crate puts `#![no_std]` in an internal module instead of only at the crate root. What should an auditor conclude?

Flag it as a correctness-of-configuration issue. It is not a proof that the arithmetic is wrong, but it shows sloppy crate-structure discipline. In a cryptographic library, even non-fatal warnings deserve cleanup because they weaken confidence in overall engineering rigor.

[TASK_TYPE=security_analysis]
[BOUNDARY=rust+crypto]
[SEVERITY=major]
Why is it useful to keep C bindings only for tests when building a clean Rust Falcon implementation?

Because that preserves the Rust implementation as the real artifact while still giving access to a trusted oracle during validation. Using C only in tests teaches faithfulness without letting the runtime library quietly depend on foreign code for correctness.

[TASK_TYPE=test_design]
[BOUNDARY=rust+crypto]
[SEVERITY=major]
After a forward FFT oracle test passes, what are the next two tests that should usually be added before declaring the transform layer stable?

Add an inverse-transform oracle test and a roundtrip test such as inverse(forward(x)) recovering x within the intended representation model. Passing only the forward test leaves too much room for one-sided faithfulness.

[TASK_TYPE=implementation]
[BOUNDARY=rust+crypto]
[SEVERITY=major]
What is the right engineering meaning of the statement "the C reference is an oracle, not a crutch"?

It means the Rust code should stand on its own and the C code should only validate equivalence, not supply hidden runtime behavior. The goal is to learn and reproduce the algorithm faithfully, not to outsource correctness to FFI.

[TASK_TYPE=attack_surface]
[BOUNDARY=rust+crypto]
[SEVERITY=major]
What risk appears if a team stops auditing after an oracle test passes and never reviews crate structure, warnings, or later refactors?

They may preserve one moment of equivalence but lose long-term engineering trust. Warnings, configuration mistakes, and later refactors can reintroduce divergence or unsafe design assumptions even if an early oracle test once passed.

[TASK_TYPE=repair]
[BOUNDARY=rust+crypto]
[SEVERITY=minor]
A Falcon Rust crate builds with warnings only because `#![no_std]` was copied into a module file. What is the correct repair?
Remove the inner-module attribute and keep `#![no_std]` only at the crate root. Then rerun the test suite to confirm the cleanup changed no arithmetic behavior.
